questions.stem: Unintended perioperative hypothermia is defined as a core temperature below which threshold?
questions.explanation: Both anesthesia textbooks define unintended perioperative hypothermia as a core temperature below 36°C. The prior 35°C key was inconsistent with the cited definitions and has been corrected to the 36°C option.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 291; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Ch. 18, printed p. 321 (complete revised answer and corrected key verified against both passages)

questions.stem: A core temperature of 35.5°C during surgery is associated with which change in morbid cardiac outcomes?
questions.explanation: The textbook associates mild perioperative hypothermia in the 35–36°C range with roughly threefold more morbid cardiac outcomes. This describes a reported population association, not an exact risk prediction for every patient at 35.5°C.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 287, 291

questions.stem: Which sensory nerve fibers predominantly carry cold-temperature signals?
questions.explanation: Cold-sensitive thermal afferents travel predominantly in thinly myelinated A-delta fibers. Warmth-sensitive signals are carried mainly by unmyelinated C fibers, with some overlap.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 287 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Which sensory nerve fibers predominantly carry warmth signals?
questions.explanation: Warmth-sensitive afferents predominantly use unmyelinated C fibers. Cold-sensitive afferents travel mainly in thinly myelinated A-delta fibers.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 287 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Through which spinal pathway does thermal sensory information ascend toward the hypothalamus?
options: Corticospinal tracts in the lateral cord
Dorsal columns in the posterior cord
Spinocerebellar tracts in the lateral cord
Spinothalamic tracts in the anterior cord
questions.explanation: Thermal afferent information ascends through spinothalamic pathways in the anterior spinal cord toward the hypothalamus. The hypothalamus integrates much of this information to coordinate thermoregulatory responses.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 287 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Which specific region is the primary thermoregulatory control center?
options: Preoptic area of the anterior hypothalamus
Supraoptic nucleus of the posterior hypothalamus
questions.explanation: The inspected passage identifies the hypothalamus as the main thermoregulatory integrator. It does not establish the specific preoptic/anterior subdivision selected by the key.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 287

questions.stem: Which family of receptor proteins is central to detecting changes in temperature?
options: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on skin nerve endings
questions.explanation: Transient receptor potential (TRP) channels are important molecular thermal sensors. Different TRP subfamilies respond preferentially to heat or cold.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 287 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: On this thermoregulatory response curve, which numbered point marks the threshold?
questions.explanation: Point 3 marks the temperature at which the cold-defense response begins. This triggering temperature is the threshold, rather than the maximal response or the gain.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 287–288

questions.stem: On this curve, the steepness of segment 2 represents what?
questions.explanation: The magnitude of the slope of segment 2 represents gain: the change in response intensity per degree of temperature change. Maximum intensity is represented by the upper plateau, not the sloping segment.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 287–288

questions.stem: A drug shifts point 3 on this curve to a lower core temperature without changing segment 2. What has the drug done?
options: Lowered the threshold; the response starts at a colder temperature
Raised the threshold; the response starts sooner
Raised the gain; the response grows stronger with each °C
Lowered the maximum intensity of the response
questions.explanation: Moving point 3 to a lower temperature delays activation until the patient is colder. An unchanged segment-2 slope means gain is unchanged.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 287–288

questions.stem: Which three functional components make up thermoregulation?
options: Afferent input, central control, efferent response
questions.explanation: Thermoregulation consists of afferent temperature sensing, central integration, and efferent responses. Together, these components detect thermal changes and adjust heat production or loss.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 287 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Which autonomic nerve fibers mediate sweating?
questions.explanation: Sweat glands receive postganglionic sympathetic fibers that release acetylcholine. This cholinergic pathway supports evaporative heat loss.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 288 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: If ambient temperature exceeds core temperature but sweat can still evaporate, which response can continue to remove body heat?
questions.explanation: When the environment is hotter than the body, radiation and convection do not provide net cooling. Evaporation of sweat can still dissipate heat if the air permits evaporation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 288 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Which mediator is NOT listed among those involved in active cutaneous vasodilation?
questions.explanation: The cited active-vasodilation list includes nitric oxide, vasoactive intestinal peptide, and substance P. Norepinephrine is not in that list; adrenergic signaling is instead associated with cold-defense vasoconstriction.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 288

questions.stem: Which thermoregulatory defenses are generally the strongest in an awake person?
questions.explanation: Behavioral responses, such as changing clothing or moving to a warmer or cooler environment, are the strongest thermoregulatory defenses. General anesthesia suppresses these voluntary adjustments.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed pp 288–289 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Which receptors mediate cold-induced arteriovenous shunt vasoconstriction in the skin?
questions.explanation: Cold-induced cutaneous arteriovenous shunt constriction is mediated by alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic receptors. This response reduces peripheral blood flow and helps conserve core heat.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 288 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: By approximately how much can shivering increase metabolic heat production?
questions.explanation: Shivering increases skeletal-muscle heat production by approximately 50% to 100%. This thermogenic response also increases metabolic oxygen requirements.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 288 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: According to the textbook, by how much can postanesthetic shivering increase oxygen demand?
questions.explanation: The cited textbook reports that postanesthetic shivering can increase oxygen demand by 135% to 468%. This may place substantial stress on patients with limited cardiopulmonary reserve.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 291 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Shivering occurs over which core temperature range?
questions.explanation: Shivering increases metabolic heat production, but its threshold changes with anesthesia and other conditions. The inspected passage does not verify 32–35°C as a universal range.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 288

questions.stem: A trauma patient's core temp is 30.5°C and there is no shivering. What best explains this?
options: The patient has reached thermal neutrality
Shivering never occurs in adults under GA
Shivering is blocked by the trauma itself
questions.explanation: Absent shivering in a cold trauma patient does not by itself identify the cause. The inspected passage does not establish a universal 32°C cutoff for cessation, so this explanation remains unresolved.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 288

questions.stem: Which is NOT a listed downside of shivering?
questions.explanation: Shivering can substantially increase oxygen demand and metabolic work. The complete claim about intracranial pressure was not verified in the inspected passages, so the full answer set remains flagged.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Which mechanism is the principal source of cold-induced heat production in newborns?
options: Increased voluntary muscle tone and movement
Active cutaneous vasodilation of the trunk
Shivering of large skeletal muscle groups
questions.explanation: Newborns rely on nonshivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue because their shivering response is immature. Brown fat generates heat without sustained skeletal-muscle contraction.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 288 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Which adrenergic receptor primarily mediates brown-fat nonshivering thermogenesis?
questions.explanation: Beta-3 adrenergic stimulation activates nonshivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue. This process uses thermogenin to release energy as heat.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 288 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: What is the function of thermogenin in brown adipose tissue?
options: Constricts skin vessels to hold heat
Increases ATP production for muscle contraction
Uncouples oxidation so substrate becomes heat directly
questions.explanation: Thermogenin is an uncoupling protein that allows energy from substrate oxidation to be released as heat. This bypasses normal conservation of much of that energy as ATP.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 288 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Approximately how much can nonshivering thermogenesis increase an infant's heat production?
questions.explanation: Brown-fat nonshivering thermogenesis can approximately double heat production in infants. Its effect on heat production is much smaller in adults.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 288 (complete revised answer verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: What is the purpose of piloerection?
options: Trapping a warm layer of air next to the skin
Increasing radiant heat loss from the skin
Increasing sweat evaporation from the skin
Stimulating brown fat beneath the skin
questions.explanation: The current key proposes insulation by trapping air next to the skin. A passage verifying this mechanism was not located in the uploaded textbook material examined, so the answer remains unverified.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13 (reading reference only; exact supporting passage not located)

questions.stem: On this core temperature curve after induction of GA, which numbered phase is caused by redistribution?
questions.explanation: Phase 1 is the rapid fall caused by redistribution of heat from the core to cooler peripheral tissues. Anesthetic vasodilation reduces the usual separation of those thermal compartments.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: What drives the slope of numbered phase 2 on this curve?
options: Heat loss exceeding metabolic heat production
Redistribution of heat from core to periphery
Shivering at the start of surgery
questions.explanation: Phase 2 reflects heat loss exceeding metabolic heat production. This slower decline differs from the initial rapid redistribution phase.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: Which thermoregulatory mechanism can contribute to numbered phase 3 on this general-anesthesia temperature curve?
options: Return of behavioral responses as anesthesia lightens
Increased metabolic rate from the volatile anesthetic
Sweating stopping once core temp falls below 36°C
Vasoconstriction once the lowered threshold is reached
questions.explanation: Vasoconstriction can conserve core heat after the lowered cold-defense threshold is reached. The textbook also allows a passive thermal steady state, so a plateau alone does not prove vasoconstriction.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: In the first phase after induction, core temperature typically falls by about how much?
questions.explanation: The textbook describes an initial fall of approximately 0.5–1.5°C after induction. Redistribution is the main mechanism, and the size of the fall varies with the starting core-to-peripheral gradient.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 288–289

questions.stem: During the linear phase of GA hypothermia, core temp falls at about what rate?
questions.explanation: The cited description estimates the slower linear decline at about 0.3°C per hour. This is an illustrative rate, not a fixed trajectory for every operation or warming strategy.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: General anesthesia decreases metabolic rate by about how much?
questions.explanation: The textbook describes a 20–30% reduction in metabolic rate during general anesthesia. Reduced heat production contributes to continued cooling when environmental heat loss exceeds production.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: During the first hour after induction, core temp drops about 1.5°C mainly because of what?
options: Conduction to the cold OR table surface
Radiant heat loss to the cold OR walls
Redistribution of heat from core to periphery
Evaporation from the airway and skin prep
questions.explanation: Anesthetic vasodilation allows warm core blood to mix with cooler peripheral tissues. This redistribution explains the early core-temperature fall better than any single external heat-loss pathway listed.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: If the OR were kept at 37°C, about what would the patient's core temp be after one hour of GA?
options: 37°C, since there is no gradient to the room
questions.explanation: Redistribution can lower core temperature even when external heat loss is limited. The inspected passage does not support predicting exactly 35.5°C after one hour in a 37°C operating room.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: Volatile anesthetics have which effect on thermoregulatory thresholds?
options: Lower the sweating threshold markedly, with no effect on cold responses
Little effect on sweating, but lower vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds
Raise the vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds
questions.explanation: Volatile anesthetics have relatively little effect on the sweating threshold but substantially lower vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds. The widened interthreshold range permits greater core-temperature drift.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: How do volatile agents, propofol, and opioids affect cold-response thresholds? Select 2.
questions.explanation: Volatile agents, propofol, and opioids lower both vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds. They therefore delay cold-defense responses until a lower core temperature is reached.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: How does neuraxial anesthesia compare with GA in its effect on thermoregulation?
options: It has minimal effect because the brain is unaffected
It improves cold responses below the block
It impairs thermoregulation to about the same extent
questions.explanation: The cited text describes neuraxial anesthesia as impairing thermoregulation to a similar extent as general anesthesia. The mechanisms include reduced cold discomfort, lower central thresholds, and blocked autonomic responses.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: The reduction in vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds with neuraxial anesthesia is proportional to what?
questions.explanation: The impairment increases with dermatomal block height. A larger blocked region removes more thermal input and autonomic response capacity.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: Why may core temperature fail to plateau during neuraxial anesthesia?
options: Redistribution is absent because the block causes no vasodilation
Peripheral vasoconstriction below the block is inhibited
questions.explanation: Neuraxial blockade inhibits peripheral vasoconstriction, so the heat-conserving response that may produce a plateau is impaired. Core temperature can therefore continue to fall.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 290

questions.stem: A patient under spinal anesthesia is 35°C but says she feels warm. What best explains this?
options: Absent tonic cold signals from the blocked area are read as warmth
Her core temperature reading is falsely low
The spinal raised her vasoconstriction threshold above normal
questions.explanation: Blocked tonic cold signals may be interpreted centrally as relative warmth. A patient can therefore feel comfortable or warm despite measured hypothermia.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: Which are mechanisms by which neuraxial anesthesia impairs thermoregulation? Select 3.
options: Raised vasoconstriction threshold proportional to block height
Impaired autonomic defenses below the block
questions.explanation: Neuraxial anesthesia lowers vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds and blocks autonomic defenses below the block. Patients may feel relatively warm despite falling core temperature because cold afferent input is reduced.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 289

questions.stem: Which mechanism accounts for most intraoperative heat loss?
questions.explanation: Radiation is the largest route of intraoperative heat loss, accounting for approximately 40% in the textbook example. The proportion varies with exposed surface area and the temperature of surrounding surfaces.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 290–291

questions.stem: Which mechanism is the second largest source of intraoperative heat loss?
questions.explanation: Convection transfers heat from the patient to surrounding moving air and accounts for approximately 30% of intraoperative heat loss in the textbook example. It ranks second after radiation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Evaporation accounts for about what share of intraoperative heat loss?
questions.explanation: Evaporation accounts for approximately 8%–10% of intraoperative heat loss in the textbook example. Water vapor leaving open cavities and the respiratory tract carries latent heat away from the body.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Radiant heat loss is proportional to the temperature difference raised to what power?
questions.explanation: The fourth-power dependence concerns absolute temperatures. The stem’s wording risks confusing the difference of fourth powers with the fourth power of a temperature difference, so the formula needs correction against a precise supporting passage.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 290–291

questions.stem: Infusing a liter of cold IV fluid causes heat loss mainly by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Cold IV fluid absorbs heat through direct contact with blood, producing conductive heat loss. Larger infused volumes and larger fluid-to-body temperature differences increase the thermal burden.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Covering the patient with drapes most effectively reduces which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Drapes limit heat transfer to moving air immediately around the patient. Among the listed choices, that effect is convection.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: On this figure, which numbered arrow represents conduction?
questions.explanation: Arrow 4 shows direct heat transfer to the surface in contact with the patient. This is conduction.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Which numbered mechanism on this figure causes the most intraoperative heat loss?
questions.explanation: Mechanism 3 represents radiation, the largest route of environmental heat loss in the cited perioperative description. The relative contribution varies with exposure and surrounding surface temperatures.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 290–291

questions.stem: A long open laparotomy most increases heat loss through which numbered mechanism?
questions.explanation: Mechanism 1 represents evaporation. An open abdominal cavity increases exposed moist surfaces from which water and latent heat can be lost.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Air currents around the patient cause loss through which numbered mechanism?
questions.explanation: Mechanism 2 depicts convection. Moving air carries heat away from the warm air layer next to the patient.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Which change contributes to hypothermia-associated coagulopathy?
options: Reduced platelet aggregation and impaired coagulation-enzyme activity
questions.explanation: Mild hypothermia impairs platelet aggregation and slows enzymes in the coagulation cascade. These changes contribute to greater bleeding and transfusion risk.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 291 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: A temperature drop from 37 to 35.5°C increases average blood loss by about how much?
questions.explanation: Hypothermia impairs platelet and coagulation-enzyme function and is associated with greater bleeding. The inspected text does not support a fixed additional 500 mL for every 1.5°C decrease.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: A hypothermic patient is oozing diffusely, but PT/PTT are normal. Why?
options: PT/PTT are falsely prolonged at low temperatures
Hypothermia only affects platelets, not clotting factors
Hypothermia causes no coagulopathy when the core is above 34°C
Labs warm the sample to 37°C, hiding the hypothermic coagulopathy
questions.explanation: Hypothermia can impair coagulation even when a laboratory result appears reassuring. The specific sample-warming explanation for normal PT/PTT was not established by the inspected passage.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: A drop from 37 to 35°C raises surgical site infection risk by about how much?
questions.explanation: The cited colorectal-surgery study found roughly threefold more wound infections with mild hypothermia. This supports the 2–3-fold choice as a study-based association, not a universal prediction for each patient.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Which mechanisms explain higher SSI risk with hypothermia? Select 3.
options: Decreased O2 delivery to the wound
Increased O2 delivery to the wound
Vasodilation flooding the wound with neutrophils
questions.explanation: Cold-induced vasoconstriction reduces wound oxygen delivery, and hypothermia can impair immune function. The complete three-choice set concerning superoxide production and neutrophil delivery was not independently verified.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Intraoperative temperature falling to 35°C increases hospital stay by about how long?
questions.explanation: The inspected text associates hypothermia with prolonged hospital stay. It does not establish a fixed 2.5-day increase for reaching 35°C.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Normothermia compared with 35°C reduces cardiac morbidity by about how much?
questions.explanation: Hypothermia is associated with increased cardiac morbidity in the cited discussion. The exact 55% reduction stated in the key was not verified and cannot be inferred directly from a threefold association.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Which mechanism described in the textbook can contribute to hypothermia-associated myocardial injury?
options: Increased blood pressure and heart rate associated with catecholamine release
A protective decrease in oxygen demand from shivering
Direct cooling inevitably causing infarction and asystole
questions.explanation: Hypothermia is associated with increased catecholamines, heart rate, and blood pressure. Those changes can increase myocardial stress; shivering can also add oxygen demand.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Which outcome is NOT included in the adverse-effect discussion of perioperative hypothermia in Anesthesia Equipment, Chapter 13?
questions.explanation: The cited adverse-effect discussion includes cardiac morbidity, prolonged drug effects, and wound infection. DVT/PE is not included in that list; this does not establish that hypothermia has no possible relationship to thrombosis.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: How does hypothermia affect MAC?
options: It has no effect on MAC
questions.explanation: Hypothermia decreases minimum alveolar concentration and therefore lowers the concentration of inhaled anesthetic required for immobility. The magnitude should not be inferred from this directional relationship.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 7, printed p. 81

questions.stem: At 34–35°C, by approximately how much does the cited study report atracurium duration is prolonged compared with normothermia?
questions.explanation: The temperature-monitoring chapter reports that atracurium duration is prolonged by about 60% at 34–35°C. It separately reports that vecuronium duration doubles after a 2°C reduction, so the drugs should not be assigned the same estimate.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 291 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Per the Wolpaw lecture, MAC decreases by about how much per 1°C drop?
questions.explanation: Hypothermia decreases MAC. The keyed 15% decrease per degree was not verified in the inspected textbook passage and remains a numerical claim requiring review.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 7, printed p. 81

questions.stem: Which three adverse effects of mild perioperative hypothermia are described in the textbook? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Mild hypothermia impairs platelet function and coagulation, increases wound-infection risk, and slows drug metabolism. It may therefore increase bleeding and delay recovery rather than improve either outcome.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 291 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: How does hypothermia affect hepatic drug metabolism?
options: It has no effect on hepatic enzymes
It slows metabolism, prolonging drug effects
It speeds metabolism, shortening drug effects
It speeds only phase II reactions
questions.explanation: Hypothermia reduces hepatic and other enzyme activity, decreasing drug metabolism. Drug effects and recovery may therefore be prolonged.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Postanesthetic shivering occurs in up to what share of patients?
questions.explanation: Ehrenwerth reports postanesthetic shivering in up to 40% of patients. Shivering causes discomfort and can substantially increase oxygen demand.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: Which patients have a higher risk of unintended perioperative hypothermia? Select 2.
options: Middle-aged adults with normal fluid shifts
questions.explanation: Extremes of age and extensive burns increase the risk of unintended perioperative hypothermia. Other listed risks include prolonged surgery, major fluid shifts, and severe trauma.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: On this ECG, which numbered deflection is characteristic of hypothermia?
questions.explanation: Deflection 3 labels the T-wave region in the supplied drawing, not a clearly identified J wave. The figure therefore does not support the intended hypothermia finding and needs replacement or correction.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13 (reading reference only; exact supporting passage not located)

questions.stem: The Osborn wave is usually not seen until core temperature falls to about what?
questions.explanation: The current key proposes a 32°C threshold for seeing an Osborn wave. An exact supporting passage was not located, so this cutoff remains unverified.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13 (reading reference only; exact supporting passage not located)

questions.stem: What is another name for the J wave seen in hypothermia?
questions.explanation: The key identifies Osborn wave as the alternative name. A specific supporting passage was not located in the uploaded books examined, so no printed-page verification is claimed.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13 (reading reference only; exact supporting passage not located)

questions.stem: Compared with an equal degree of hypothermia, hyperthermia is:
questions.explanation: Ehrenwerth describes hyperthermia as more dangerous than a similar degree of hypothermia. Elevated temperature increases metabolic demand and cardiovascular stress and can injure multiple organ systems.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of intraoperative hyperthermia?
questions.explanation: Ehrenwerth identifies iatrogenic overwarming as the most common cause of intraoperative hyperthermia. It is especially important during long procedures and in infants and children.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: Four hours into a case under a full-body forced-air warmer, temp has slowly risen to 38.1°C. EtCO2 and HR are stable. FIRST action?
options: Turn down or remove the forced-air warmer and recheck
Switch to TIVA, give dantrolene, and call for the MH cart
questions.explanation: A gradual temperature rise during active warming with stable CO2 and heart rate makes excessive external heating a reasonable first consideration. Reduce warming and reassess the temperature trend while continuing to evaluate for other causes if the rise persists or additional signs appear.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: Which finding best distinguishes early MH from iatrogenic overwarming?
options: A forced-air warmer set to high
Flushed, warm skin over the trunk
Core temperature that reaches 38°C late in the case
questions.explanation: Malignant hyperthermia causes excessive CO2 production, so rising end-tidal CO2 despite increased ventilation is an important warning sign. Simple overwarming does not ordinarily produce the same hypermetabolic pattern.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 36, printed p. 842; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: Which are listed consequences of hyperthermia? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Hyperthermia increases metabolic demand and cardiovascular stress. Severe elevations can cause coagulopathy, renal and hepatic dysfunction, neuropathy, and seizures.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: Which drug class is associated with neuroleptic malignant syndrome in the cited textbook discussion?
questions.explanation: Antipsychotics are associated with neuroleptic malignant syndrome. The inspected text supports that drug-class association but not the original fixed 2% incidence.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 14, printed p. 215

questions.stem: Stopping which drug can trigger NMS?
questions.explanation: The key proposes levodopa withdrawal as a trigger. The specific withdrawal syndrome was not independently verified in the inspected passages.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13 (reading reference only; exact supporting passage not located)

questions.stem: An antiemetic linked to NMS in the lecture is:
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide is the current keyed antiemetic. Its specific NMS association was not established by the inspected passages; a serotonin-toxicity drug table cannot verify that separate claim.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13 (reading reference only; exact supporting passage not located)

questions.stem: Typical onset of NMS is:
questions.explanation: NMS onset depends on the exposure and clinical context. The keyed 24–72-hour range with extension to two weeks was not verified in the inspected material.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13 (reading reference only; exact supporting passage not located)

questions.stem: What is the dantrolene dosing range listed for NMS?
options: 2.5 mg/kg IV push repeated to 10 mg/kg
questions.explanation: The inspected text notes that dantrolene may be useful in NMS. It does not verify the keyed daily NMS dose; a malignant-hyperthermia dosing regimen would not establish this separate treatment schedule.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 36, printed p. 843

questions.stem: According to the cited textbook, serotonin-toxicity symptoms may appear over which interval after a serotonergic exposure or change?
questions.explanation: The cited text describes serotonin-toxicity symptoms appearing within minutes to 24 hours after an exposure or serotonergic change. Timing alone does not establish the diagnosis.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 14, printed p. 213

questions.stem: A patient on an MAOI gets meperidine in PACU and develops fever, clonus, and hyperreflexia within 2 hours. Which treatment is least likely to help?
questions.explanation: Stopping the offending agents, supportive care, and benzodiazepines are described treatments for serotonin toxicity. The inspected passage does not directly establish the complete comparative claim that dantrolene is least likely to help.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 14, printed p. 213

questions.stem: Which three medications are explicitly listed in Nurse Anesthesia Table 14.9 as implicated in serotonin syndrome? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Table 14.9 lists linezolid, methylene blue, and fentanyl among agents implicated in serotonin syndrome. The prior options included metoclopramide as an unkeyed choice and ritonavir as a keyed choice, despite the table listing the former but not the latter.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Ch. 14, printed p. 214 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes serotonin syndrome from NMS?
options: Hyperreflexia and clonus with abrupt onset
Recent exposure to a psychiatric medication
questions.explanation: Clonus and hyperreflexia are characteristic findings in serotonin toxicity, and onset can be rapid. The full comparison with NMS remains unresolved without a specific comparative passage.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 14, printed pp. 213–214

questions.stem: In severe serotonin syndrome not controlled by benzodiazepines, the lecture suggests considering what?
questions.explanation: Severe serotonin syndrome may require sedation, tracheal intubation, and neuromuscular paralysis. Paralysis must be accompanied by adequate sedation and ventilatory support.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 14, printed p.213

questions.stem: Prewarming before induction reduces redistribution hypothermia by doing what?
options: Raising the vasoconstriction threshold before induction
questions.explanation: Prewarming raises peripheral tissue temperature and reduces the core-to-peripheral temperature gradient. Less heat therefore redistributes from the core after anesthetic-induced vasodilation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: What prewarming interval is described in the textbook as preventing redistribution hypothermia before induction?
questions.explanation: Prewarming the skin reduces the core-to-peripheral temperature gradient before induction. The cited text describes benefit from 30 minutes of prewarming.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: Per Wolpaw, how long does prewarming need to be fully effective?
questions.explanation: The textbook describes effective 30-minute prewarming and benefit with 60 minutes in another study. A two-hour research protocol does not establish that two hours is required for full effectiveness.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 292–293

questions.stem: What ambient temperature is recommended for prewarming children in the induction room and OR?
questions.explanation: Ehrenwerth describes raising ambient temperature to 26°C for 30–40 minutes as a safe and effective method of prewarming children. This is a reported approach rather than a requirement for every child or warming system.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: One liter of room-temperature crystalloid lowers mean body temperature by about how much?
questions.explanation: Ehrenwerth estimates that infusing 1 L of crystalloid at 21°C into a body at 37°C lowers mean body temperature by approximately 0.25°C. The temperature change depends on the infused fluid temperature, volume, and patient heat capacity.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 291

questions.stem: IV fluids should be warmed to what range?
questions.explanation: Warming large or rapidly infused fluid volumes reduces the heat burden from cold infusions. The inspected passage does not verify 38–42°C as a general fluid-temperature target.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 293

questions.stem: Per the lecture, what is the most basic method for maintaining normothermia in the OR?
options: Forced-air warming over the upper body
questions.explanation: Increasing ambient room temperature reduces the gradient driving heat loss to the surroundings. Ehrenwerth describes this as the most basic approach to maintaining normothermia in the OR.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 294

questions.stem: What is the easiest method to decrease cutaneous heat loss?
options: Passive insulation of the skin surface
questions.explanation: Passive insulation is the simplest way to reduce cutaneous heat loss. Blankets and drapes retain heat but do not supply sustained active warming.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 294

questions.stem: Warm cotton blankets reduce radiant heat loss by up to about how much?
questions.explanation: Cotton blankets can reduce radiant heat loss by as much as 30% in the evidence summarized by Ehrenwerth. Their benefit depends on how much skin is covered, and passive insulation may be insufficient during major surgery.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 294

questions.stem: Which listed noninvasive technique actively transfers substantial heat over a large skin surface during major surgery?
questions.explanation: Forced-air warming actively transfers heat across a large covered skin surface. Among the listed noninvasive choices, it provides more effective active warming than passive insulation or warmed respiratory gas.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 294–295

questions.stem: Which listed technique uses an extracorporeal heat exchanger to rewarm circulating blood and can reverse profound hypothermia?
questions.explanation: Cardiopulmonary bypass can transfer heat directly to circulating blood through its heat exchanger. The cited discussion describes its ability to actively cool and rewarm patients, including reversal of profound hypothermia.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 295

questions.stem: Why can a circulating-water warming mattress be less effective and less safe beneath the patient than over the patient?
options: Top warmers block conduction to the table
Heat rises, so an underbody warmer mostly warms the table
Body weight compresses the tissue, so less blood flows there
questions.explanation: Pressure under the patient reduces local perfusion where a warming mattress contacts the skin. This limits heat distribution and increases the risk of thermal injury.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 294–295

questions.stem: Forced-air warmers work by doing what?
options: Transferring heat by conduction from heated coils in the blanket
Reducing evaporation by humidifying the skin
Raising core temperature by warming inspired gas
Preventing radiant loss while transferring heat by convection
questions.explanation: Forced-air blankets reduce radiative heat loss while transferring heat to the patient by convection. Their effectiveness depends on the surface area covered and contact between the blanket and patient.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 295

questions.stem: According to the temperature-monitoring chapter, a forced-air warming system can raise core temperature at approximately what rate?
questions.explanation: The chapter reports that forced-air warming can raise core temperature by approximately 0.75°C per hour. The former forced-air versus cardiopulmonary-bypass comparison was not supported by the cited passage.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 295 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: For severe hypothermia with cardiac instability when ECMO is unavailable, the rewarming table lists which technique (about 9°C/hr)?
questions.explanation: Cardiopulmonary bypass can provide active core rewarming. The specific rewarming-table indication and approximately 9°C-per-hour rate were not verified in the inspected textbook material.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 295

questions.stem: Which rewarming technique in the table provides cardiac support at about 6°C/hr?
questions.explanation: The key identifies venoarterial ECMO as the support technique. The claimed table entry and 6°C-per-hour rate were not located, so the complete answer remains unverified.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 295

questions.stem: An esophageal stethoscope with a temperature probe is an example of what?
questions.explanation: An esophageal stethoscope with a temperature sensor is an example of a thermistor-based probe. Thermistors use temperature-dependent electrical conductivity in a metal-oxide semiconductor.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 296

questions.stem: Thermocouples and thermistors are accurate to about what range?
questions.explanation: Ehrenwerth describes thermistor accuracy of 0.1–0.2°C and carefully made thermocouple accuracy of about 0.1°C. These devices convert temperature-dependent electrical properties into a monitor reading.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 296–298

questions.stem: Why are liquid crystal skin thermometers poor choices intraoperatively?
options: They are too expensive for routine OR use
Skin and core temps diverge during rapid changes
questions.explanation: Liquid-crystal strips measure skin temperature, which may diverge substantially from core temperature. That discrepancy is especially important during rapid physiologic temperature changes.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 298

questions.stem: Which listed site is classified as a reliable core-temperature site even during rapid thermal changes in the cited textbook?
questions.explanation: Distal esophageal temperature is a reliable core measurement when the sensor is properly positioned. Rectal, axillary, and bladder measurements have additional limitations during rapid thermal changes.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 299

questions.stem: Which site is the reference standard for core-temperature measurement in the cited textbook?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary arterial blood temperature is the reference standard described in the text. Other properly positioned core sites can closely approximate it, but the question does not establish high internal-jugular temperature as an interchangeable standard.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 299

questions.stem: According to Figure 13.20 in Anesthesia Equipment, which three sites are classified as core temperature sites rather than intermediate sites? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Figure 13.20 classifies pulmonary artery, tympanic membrane, and nasopharynx among core sites. It places bladder, oral, and rectal measurements among intermediate sites that can lag during rapid temperature changes.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 13, printed p. 299 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: During rapid rewarming on bypass, which site is least reliable for core temperature?
questions.explanation: Rectal temperature responds slowly to rapid changes in central blood temperature. This lag makes it unreliable for tracking rapid cooling or rewarming.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 299

questions.stem: Which site is decent for core temp but carries a bleeding risk?
questions.explanation: Nasopharyngeal temperature closely reflects brain temperature, but probe placement can cause epistaxis. Bleeding and displacement are important limitations, especially in anticoagulated patients.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 299

questions.stem: When is human body temperature normally lowest?
questions.explanation: Core temperature varies with circadian rhythm. The inspected passage does not establish the exact 4–8 a.m. interval selected by the key.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 287

questions.stem: About what share of postoperative fevers are NOT caused by infection?
questions.explanation: Postoperative fever has multiple possible causes. The inspected passage does not verify that 67% of postoperative fevers are noninfectious.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: Which statement about fever in hospitalized patients is correct?
options: All fevers above 38.5°C should be treated
Higher fevers reliably point to a bacterial infection source
Fever severity does not correlate with likelihood of infection
Treating fever below 40°C is always beneficial
questions.explanation: Temperature alone does not establish the cause of fever. The claimed absence of a relationship between fever severity and infection probability still needs a specific supporting passage.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: Compared with GA alone, what does neuraxial anesthesia change about the temperature curve?
options: There is no initial drop, only a linear decline
The initial drop is larger, then temperature rises
Temperature rises after the drop because vasodilation is blocked
The initial drop is similar, but the plateau may not develop
questions.explanation: Neuraxial anesthesia causes initial redistribution and continued heat loss, but the plateau seen with general anesthesia may fail to develop. Vasoconstriction is inhibited below the block and its central threshold is lowered.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed pp. 289–290

questions.stem: Before a long case, prewarming for 30 minutes is planned. Which effect is expected?
options: Prevention of the linear phase entirely
A rise in core temperature that offsets the linear phase
No change in the initial drop, but a faster plateau
A smaller initial drop in core temperature after induction
questions.explanation: Prewarming warms peripheral tissue and narrows the core-to-peripheral temperature gradient. This reduces the initial redistribution-related fall in core temperature after induction.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 13, printed p. 292

questions.stem: An inappropriate intention or action, often from lack of training or knowledge, is which error type?
questions.explanation: A mistake involves an unsuitable plan, intention, or action, often because knowledge or training is inadequate. It differs from a slip, in which an appropriate intention is carried out incorrectly or at the wrong time.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: The correct intention carried out at the wrong time is which error type?
questions.explanation: A slip occurs when an appropriate intended action is performed incorrectly or at an inappropriate time. It often affects familiar tasks performed with little conscious attention.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: A provider stays convinced the falling SpO2 is probe artifact and keeps repositioning it while the patient desaturates from a disconnect. Which error is this?
questions.explanation: Fixation occurs when a clinician persists with an interpretation or action despite evidence that the situation has changed. Repeatedly dismissing true desaturation as artifact prevents reconsideration of a potentially dangerous cause.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: A provider who suspects light anesthesia looks only at the rising HR and ignores the falling BP. Which error is this?
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias favors information that supports an existing hypothesis while discounting contradictory findings. Attending only to tachycardia while ignoring hypotension illustrates this selective interpretation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: Out of habit from the previous case, a provider pushes the routine induction sequence on a patient who was supposed to have an awake fiberoptic. Which error type fits best?
questions.explanation: A capture error occurs when a familiar routine takes over at the wrong time. Here, the usual induction sequence displaces the planned awake airway approach.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: A provider believes the descending bellows will collapse with a disconnect, so she misses a disconnection. Which error type is this?
questions.explanation: A representational error arises from an incorrect mental model of how a system works. Misunderstanding the behavior of a descending bellows can therefore lead to misinterpretation of a disconnect.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: Misclassifying the situation, such as treating a ventilator in standby as if it were ventilating, is which error?
questions.explanation: A mode error involves misclassifying the system’s current operating state. Assuming that a ventilator in standby is delivering breaths is an example.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: "Give the usual dose" without stating drug or amount is an example of which error?
questions.explanation: A description error involves an ambiguous or incomplete statement of the intended action. An order for “the usual dose” omits essential information about the drug and amount.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: Failing to activate the needed action, such as not starting ventilation after intubation, is which error?
questions.explanation: Faulty activation includes failing to initiate the appropriate action or activating an inappropriate one. Omitting the start of ventilation after airway placement fits this category.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: Automatic actions called into play by an ongoing sequence, though wrong for the situation, define which error?
questions.explanation: A data-driven error occurs when an ongoing action sequence triggers an automatic response that is inappropriate for the situation. The action is cued by the sequence rather than a deliberate assessment of current needs.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: During an anesthesia crisis, a team continues the same treatment despite evidence that it is failing. Which cognitive error should crisis-resource-management training help the team recognize?
questions.explanation: Continuing an ineffective plan despite contradictory evidence is a fixation error, often described as tunnel vision. Crisis-resource-management training encourages reassessment and communication to interrupt this pattern.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Ch. 60, printed pp. 1364–1365 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Which error types involve the provider's thinking getting stuck or biased? Select 2.
questions.explanation: Fixation keeps the clinician committed to a failing interpretation or course of action. Confirmation bias reinforces that commitment by favoring supporting evidence and overlooking conflicting findings.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 372

questions.stem: Mishearing the surgeon and giving the wrong antibiotic is an example of which cause of error?
questions.explanation: Mishearing a request and administering the wrong antibiotic illustrates a communication failure associated with noise. The textbook uses this example to show how environmental conditions can contribute to human error.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: Rapid administration of vancomycin or protamine is the lecture's example of which cause of error?
questions.explanation: Ehrenwerth uses rapid vancomycin or protamine administration as an example of error related to insufficient training or experience. The category refers to the underlying knowledge or skill gap, rather than proving the cause in every actual event.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: A syringe swap during a critical event illustrates which cause of error?
questions.explanation: Stress can disrupt familiar actions during a critical event and contribute to a syringe or ampoule swap. The textbook lists that scenario under stress-related human error.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: Failing to ventilate when coming off cardiopulmonary bypass is the lecture's example of which cause?
questions.explanation: Failing to ventilate when separating from cardiopulmonary bypass is the textbook’s example of task complexity contributing to error. Multiple simultaneous tasks can compete for attention during this transition.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: A circuit disconnects when personnel move equipment around the patient. Which cause of error is this?
questions.explanation: A circuit disconnect caused by movement of equipment or personnel illustrates workspace constraints. Crowding and poor arrangement can create hazards even when individual actions seem routine.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: A provider misses a developing event while hand-charting vital signs. Which cause of error does the lecture assign?
options: Task complexity at a critical point
questions.explanation: Manually recording vital signs can draw attention away from detecting a developing event. Ehrenwerth categorizes this example as a mismatch between human capabilities and machine functions.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: The lecture's equipment-design example of error is which event?
options: A circuit disconnect when equipment is moved around the bed
The laryngoscope bulb going out during intubation
questions.explanation: Ehrenwerth uses a laryngoscope light failing during intubation as an example under poor equipment design. This is a representative textbook category, not a determination of the cause of every light failure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: After disabling a noisy alarm, a provider fails to recognize a critical event. Which cause of error is this?
questions.explanation: Frequent false or noisy alarms can lead clinicians to disable or disregard them. The resulting loss of warning can delay recognition of a true critical event.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: "A coherent mental model of the current state of a complex system, including prior conditions and implications for future states" defines what?
questions.explanation: Situation awareness combines an understanding of the current system state with how it developed and what may happen next. It goes beyond noticing an isolated monitor value.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: A state of readiness to detect and respond to changes, "sustained attention," defines what?
questions.explanation: Vigilance is readiness to detect and respond to changes in the monitored environment. It requires sustained attention even when important signals occur infrequently.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: Observing one or more data streams to detect specified changes that occur at random intervals defines what?
questions.explanation: Monitoring involves observing one or more data streams for specified changes that may occur unpredictably. It is a task that depends on vigilance rather than a guarantee that all changes will be detected.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: Choosing between alternative diagnoses or actions based on judgments defines what?
questions.explanation: Decision-making is choosing among possible diagnoses or actions using the judgments formed from available information. The best choice may need to change as new information appears.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: Gaining awareness or understanding through the senses defines what?
questions.explanation: Perception is becoming aware of or understanding information through the senses. Interpretation and decision-making then use that perceived information to guide action.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: Which are individual (human) factors known to affect vigilance? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Sleep deprivation, circadian disruption from shift work, and boredom are individual factors that can impair vigilance. They can reduce sustained attention even when equipment and environmental conditions are adequate.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 374

questions.stem: Which are environmental factors affecting vigilance? Select 2.
questions.explanation: Noise and ambient lighting are environmental factors that affect vigilance. Fatigue and personality are individual factors, while task intrusion belongs to the task itself.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 374

questions.stem: Latent errors built into a system belong to which factor category?
questions.explanation: Latent system-induced errors are classified as system-and-equipment factors in Box 17.1. They can remain hidden until circumstances combine to produce an incident.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 374

questions.stem: Which are stated functions of alarms? Select 3.
options: Document events for the anesthesia record
Assist when stress or workload impairs detection
Allow volumes to be turned off during stable periods
Aid a fatigued or nonvigilant provider
Replace the need for continuous provider vigilance
Detect adverse conditions in the patient or equipment
questions.explanation: Alarms detect adverse conditions, support fatigued or nonvigilant providers, and assist when stress or workload impairs recognition. The textbook explicitly lists these three functions; alarms supplement rather than replace clinical monitoring.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 386

questions.stem: Which monitoring tone can communicate changes in oxygen saturation through changes in pitch?
questions.explanation: Pulse-oximeter tone pitch changes with measured oxygen saturation, allowing auditory recognition of trends. This is a specific information-coding feature, not a textbook ranking of one alarm as the most important.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 17, printed pp. 388 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Failing to hear auditory alarms while under a high visual workload is called what?
questions.explanation: Inattentional deafness is the reduced recognition of auditory alarms during high visual workload. The textbook explicitly names this phenomenon and describes the visual-attention bottleneck.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 387

questions.stem: How can alarms be designed so the clinician knows which alarm is sounding?
options: Varying pattern, pitch, tone, and frequency
Making all alarms the same loud tone
questions.explanation: Distinct patterns and acoustic properties can help identify which alarm is sounding. The textbook also cautions that evidence does not establish one universally superior alarm-tone system for the OR.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed pp. 387–388

questions.stem: High OR noise levels can have which effect on alarms?
questions.explanation: Background noise can mask alarm tones and make them harder to recognize. Reducing ambient noise can improve the effective signal-to-noise ratio.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 375

questions.stem: Per the lecture, alarm limits are most useful when set so they activate when?
options: After the provider confirms the event
Only once the condition becomes critical
questions.explanation: Alarm limits should provide warning early enough to permit intervention before a condition becomes critical. Appropriate limits depend on the patient, rate of deterioration, and measurement and response delays.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 389

questions.stem: Which must be considered when setting an alarm limit? Select 3.
options: The cost of the monitoring equipment
The number of other alarms in the room
The rate at which the variable is changing
The response time of the measurement system
questions.explanation: Alarm-limit selection must account for how quickly the variable changes, measurement-system delay, and the clinician’s correction time. The textbook additionally includes patient condition and the alarm system’s own response time.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 389

questions.stem: A sidestream gas analyzer has a long transit time. How should that affect the alarm limit you set?
options: Disable it, because delayed data are too unreliable to use
Set it to trigger later to avoid false alarms
Set it to trigger earlier to allow for the measurement delay
No change; response time does not matter
questions.explanation: A longer measurement delay leaves less time to correct a developing problem. An earlier warning threshold can compensate, provided the limit is individualized to avoid excessive false alerts.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 389

questions.stem: Deaths from alarms turned off after repeated false alerts led to recognition of what problem?
questions.explanation: Repeated false alerts can desensitize clinicians and prompt alarm deactivation, delaying recognition of real deterioration. This problem is termed alarm fatigue.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed pp. 389–390

questions.stem: Which strategies improve the signal-to-noise ratio of alarms? Select 3.
options: Silencing alarms whenever the patient seems stable
Reducing false-positive alerts through better design and maintenance
Raising every alarm volume to its maximum level
Secondary notification by pager or phone
Widening alarm limits so they rarely sound at all
Sound-absorbing material to lower background noise
questions.explanation: Better design and maintenance reduce false alerts, while quieter surroundings improve audibility. Secondary pager or phone notifications can improve alarm delivery without simply increasing bedside volume.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed pp. 389–390

questions.stem: During a crisis, a provider swaps two syringes and then keeps attributing the hypotension to "light anesthesia." Which pair of error sources is present?
options: Stress-related swap followed by fixation error
Equipment design followed by mode error
Lack of training followed by capture error
questions.explanation: A syringe swap during a crisis illustrates stress-related error. Persistently attributing contradictory findings to the same explanation then illustrates fixation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed pp. 372–373

questions.stem: Which term includes both awareness and judgment?
questions.explanation: Cognition includes both awareness and judgment. It encompasses knowing and interpreting information rather than merely detecting it.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 17, printed p. 373

questions.stem: During a difficult airway, the provider stares at the video laryngoscope screen and misses the SpO2 tone dropping. Which phenomenon best explains the miss?
options: Inattentional deafness from high visual workload
Alarm fatigue from repeated false alarms earlier
questions.explanation: High visual workload during difficult laryngoscopy can reduce recognition of an audible oxygen-saturation change. This is inattentional deafness, a phenomenon explicitly described in the textbook.
