questions.stem: A waveform changes from panel B to panel C over 30 minutes. FIRST check?
options: ETT position, looking for esophageal intubation
CO2 absorbent and unidirectional valve function
questions.explanation: The elevated inspiratory baseline in panel C suggests rebreathing. Checking the absorbent and unidirectional valves is appropriate among these choices.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 242

questions.stem: Which capnography trend panel fits cardiac arrest?
questions.explanation: The lower-left panel shows an abrupt loss of detected exhaled CO₂, which can occur with cardiac arrest. Disconnection, sampling failure, or airway problems can also produce this pattern.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 248; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 18, printed p. 318

questions.stem: Which trend panel fits return of spontaneous circulation during CPR?
questions.explanation: The lower-right panel shows a sudden rise in exhaled CO₂ during low-flow CPR conditions. This is consistent with restored pulmonary blood flow and return of spontaneous circulation, which requires clinical confirmation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 248; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 18, printed p. 318

questions.stem: Which trend panel fits hypoventilation?
questions.explanation: The upper-left panel shows progressively higher end-tidal CO₂. With other factors stable, reduced alveolar ventilation can produce this trend.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 248; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 18, printed p. 318

questions.stem: Which trend panel fits hyperventilation?
questions.explanation: The upper-right panel shows progressively lower end-tidal CO₂. With perfusion and metabolism stable, increased alveolar ventilation can cause this trend.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 248; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 18, printed p. 318

questions.stem: EtCO2 drops abruptly to near zero as in the lower-left panel while airway pressures are unchanged and the circuit is intact. What should you suspect first?
options: Hyperventilation from an increase in rate
Loss of cardiac output or massive embolism
questions.explanation: A sudden CO₂ loss with an apparently intact airway and circuit raises concern for sharply reduced pulmonary perfusion. Loss of cardiac output or a major embolic event is a possibility, not a diagnosis established by the waveform alone.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 248; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 18, printed p. 318

questions.stem: What physiologic mechanism explains how hyperventilation-induced hypocapnia can reduce intracranial pressure?
options: Lower CO2 causes cerebral vasoconstriction, lowering blood flow
Lower CO2 causes cerebral vasodilation, raising blood flow
Hyperventilation raises CO2 to protect neurons
questions.explanation: Lower PaCO₂ causes cerebral vasoconstriction and reduces cerebral blood flow, which can reduce intracranial blood volume. Excessive hypocapnia can also compromise cerebral oxygen delivery, so this is a physiologic explanation rather than a universal treatment target.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 247

questions.stem: Why is ventilation and CO₂ monitoring important during transport of a patient with raised intracranial pressure?
options: Transport monitors can’t display SpO2 reliably
EtCO2 replaces the need for an arterial line
CO2 swings change cerebral blood flow and ICP
questions.explanation: Changes in PaCO₂ can alter cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure. Capnography helps detect ventilation changes during transport, but it does not directly measure ICP or replace assessment of arterial CO₂ when needed.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed pp. 247–248

questions.stem: Under normal conditions, CO2 is excreted how?
options: As fast as it is made, with no net change
Slower than it is made, so body stores rise
In bursts during the expiratory pause
Faster than it is made, so body stores fall
questions.explanation: In a steady state, pulmonary CO₂ elimination matches total body production. If ventilation changes abruptly, body stores can temporarily make elimination differ from production.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 245

questions.stem: Which change would raise CO2 production?
options: Increased metabolism, such as fever or MH
questions.explanation: Increased metabolic activity, including fever or malignant hyperthermia, can increase CO₂ delivery and production. The resulting end-tidal value also depends on ventilation and perfusion.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 18, printed p. 318

questions.stem: Which factors interact to alter the amount of CO₂ eliminated from breath to breath? Select 3.
questions.explanation: The amount of CO₂ eliminated in each breath depends on tidal volume, dead space, and effective alveolar ventilation. These interacting factors make single-breath measurements variable.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 245

questions.stem: What can a sampling-line leak that mixes room air into the sample do to EtCO₂ accuracy?
options: Raises it falsely to arterial levels
questions.explanation: Room air entering a leaking sampling line can dilute the sampled CO₂. The displayed end-tidal value may then fail to reflect the patient’s true expired concentration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 245

questions.stem: Alveolar dead space is best described as:
questions.explanation: Alveolar dead space is ventilation reaching alveoli that receive little or no effective perfusion. That ventilation contributes little to gas exchange.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed pp. 245–246

questions.stem: Excluding external apparatus, patient physiologic dead space equals:
options: Alveolar dead space minus anatomic dead space
Tidal volume minus alveolar volume only at rest
Airway (anatomic) dead space plus alveolar dead space
questions.explanation: Patient physiologic dead space combines conducting-airway and alveolar dead space. External apparatus can add further ineffective ventilation and should be considered separately in this wording.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed pp. 245–246

questions.stem: In the textbook model with PaCO₂ unchanged, how does a large increase in alveolar dead space change the PaCO₂–EtCO₂ gradient?
options: Has no effect, since both values fall together
Reverses it, so EtCO2 exceeds PaCO2
Widens it, because EtCO2 falls while PaCO2 does not
Narrows it, because EtCO2 rises toward PaCO2
questions.explanation: In the illustrated dead-space model, low-CO₂ gas from underperfused alveoli dilutes expired gas. End-tidal CO₂ falls relative to arterial CO₂, widening the gradient.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed pp. 243–244

questions.stem: Which cause increased dead space (V/Q mismatch) that lowers EtCO2? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Pulmonary embolism, hypovolemia, and alveolar overdistension can reduce perfusion relative to ventilation. The resulting alveolar dead space can lower end-tidal CO₂ relative to arterial CO₂.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 246

questions.stem: Per the instructor, capnography changes from dead space often appear when?
options: After SpO2 has started to fall
questions.explanation: Capnography can reveal changes in ventilation and pulmonary perfusion. The inspected passages do not establish a universal timing advantage over all hemodynamic signs.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 18, printed p. 318

questions.stem: During CPR with stable minute ventilation, exceeding which approximate PETCO₂ threshold is described as indicating potentially survivable pulmonary blood flow?
questions.explanation: The cited discussion uses a value greater than approximately 10 mmHg during stable minute ventilation as evidence of potentially survivable pulmonary blood flow. It does not guarantee adequate CPR or determine prognosis by itself.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 248

questions.stem: During CPR, PETCO2 is 6 mmHg. What is the best response?
questions.explanation: Low end-tidal CO₂ during CPR should prompt assessment of compression quality and other reversible causes of low pulmonary flow. It is not, by itself, a reason to stop resuscitation or automatically increase ventilation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 248

questions.stem: Why is pulmonary embolism hard to diagnose with capnography alone?
options: Capnography can’t reflect dead space changes
PE has no effect on CO2 elimination
Baseline alveolar dead space is usually unknown
questions.explanation: The baseline alveolar dead space is often unknown, and several other conditions can reduce pulmonary perfusion. A low end-tidal value therefore cannot uniquely diagnose pulmonary embolism.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 249

questions.stem: During sedation cases, capnography helps detect what?
questions.explanation: Capnography can detect respiratory obstruction and inadequate ventilation during sedation. Supplemental oxygen can delay a fall in SpO₂ even while ventilation deteriorates.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 249

questions.stem: Functional saturation (SaO2) is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Functional saturation is O₂Hb divided by O₂Hb plus reduced hemoglobin. Dyshemoglobins are excluded from that denominator.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 253

questions.stem: Why does fractional saturation read lower than functional saturation with significant carbon monoxide?
options: Functional saturation counts COHb as oxygenated
The two values are identical in CO poisoning
Fractional includes COHb and MetHb in the denominator
questions.explanation: Fractional saturation includes COHb and MetHb in the denominator. With substantial COHb, it can therefore be lower than functional saturation for the same oxyhemoglobin concentration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 253

questions.stem: In CaO2 = 1.34 × Hb × SaO2 + 0.003 × PaO2, what does 0.003 × PaO2 represent?
questions.explanation: The term 0.003 × PaO₂ estimates oxygen dissolved in plasma; the much larger hemoglobin-bound contribution is 1.34 × Hb × SaO₂.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed. Chapter 11: Pulse Oximetry (source chapter; exact passage not individually verified)

questions.stem: Hb 10 g/dL, SaO2 100%, PaO2 100 mmHg. What is CaO2?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin-bound O₂ is 1.34 × 10 × 1.00 = 13.4 mL/dL; dissolved O₂ is 0.003 × 100 = 0.3 mL/dL. Total arterial O₂ content is about 13.7 mL/dL.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed. Chapter 11: Pulse Oximetry (source chapter; exact passage not individually verified)

questions.stem: Oxygen delivery to tissues depends on CaO2 and what?
questions.explanation: Oxygen delivery is arterial oxygen content multiplied by cardiac output (DO₂ = CaO₂ × CO, with unit conversion as needed). Raising saturation alone does not ensure delivery.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed. Chapter 11: Pulse Oximetry (source chapter; exact passage not individually verified)

questions.stem: How many O2 binding sites does each hemoglobin molecule have?
questions.explanation: Each hemoglobin molecule contains four heme groups, each capable of binding one O₂ molecule.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed. Chapter 11: Pulse Oximetry (source chapter; exact passage not individually verified)

questions.stem: The Beer-Lambert law is written as:
questions.explanation: The Beer–Lambert relation is A = εcl: absorbance equals the extinction coefficient multiplied by concentration and optical path length.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed. Chapter 11: Pulse Oximetry (source chapter; exact passage not individually verified)

questions.stem: In the Beer-Lambert law, what does "l" stand for?
questions.explanation: In the Beer–Lambert equation, l is optical path length: the distance light travels through the absorbing sample.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed. Chapter 11: Pulse Oximetry (source chapter; exact passage not individually verified)

questions.stem: Per Beer-Lambert, doubling the concentration of an absorber while holding path length constant does what to absorbance?
questions.explanation: With the extinction coefficient and path length fixed, absorbance is proportional to absorber concentration. Doubling concentration doubles absorbance.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed. Chapter 11: Pulse Oximetry (source chapter; exact passage not individually verified)

questions.stem: Which device relies on the Beer-Lambert law?
questions.explanation: Pulse oximeters estimate hemoglobin saturation from the differential absorption of red and infrared light through pulsatile tissue.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed. Chapter 11: Pulse Oximetry (source chapter; exact passage not individually verified)

questions.stem: Fetal hemoglobin has what effect on pulse oximetry?
questions.explanation: Fetal hemoglobin generally has little effect on conventional two-wavelength pulse-oximeter accuracy because its optical absorption is similar to adult hemoglobin at those wavelengths.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed. Chapter 11: Pulse Oximetry (source chapter; exact passage not individually verified)

questions.stem: Which can cause pulse oximetry errors? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Methemoglobin, colored dyes, and some nail polishes alter light absorption and may distort pulse-oximeter readings; poor perfusion and motion are additional sources of error.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed. Chapter 11: Pulse Oximetry (source chapter; exact passage not individually verified)

questions.stem: Dyshemoglobins such as methemoglobin cause errors because they:
options: They increase perfusion at the probe site
Cannot carry O2 but still absorb light
They carry O2 more efficiently than normal Hb
They are invisible to the oximeter’s light
questions.explanation: Methemoglobin and other dyshemoglobins alter optical absorption without functioning like normal oxygen-carrying hemoglobin, so two-wavelength pulse oximetry can be misleading.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed. Chapter 11: Pulse Oximetry (source chapter; exact passage not individually verified)

questions.stem: Per the instructor, which finger has the most perfusion for probe placement?
questions.explanation: Probe-site quality depends on perfusion, motion, device design, and signal strength. There is no universally preferred finger established by the cited textbook.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed. Chapter 11: Pulse Oximetry (source chapter; exact passage not individually verified)

questions.stem: How do modern oximeters reduce motion artifact?
options: Longer signal averaging and ECG synchronization
Using a single wavelength of light
Increasing the light intensity at the probe site
questions.explanation: Motion-rejection algorithms use signal processing, adaptive filtering, and sometimes pulse synchronization to distinguish arterial pulsations from artifact. Performance varies by device.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed. Chapter 11: Pulse Oximetry (source chapter; exact passage not individually verified)

questions.stem: SpO2 is determined from which signal?
questions.explanation: Some motion-resistant pulse oximeters estimate the artifact component and subtract it from the total optical signal. This signal-extraction approach helps isolate arterial pulsations; it is not the calculation used by every oximeter.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 260 (textbook passage reviewed; answer-specific caveat in audit)

questions.stem: A dependent probe position can lower SpO2 by up to how much?
questions.explanation: Dependent positioning can increase venous pulsations that contaminate the arterial optical signal. One volunteer study reported an apparent SpO₂ decrease of up to 8% when an arm was lowered.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 260 (textbook passage reviewed)

questions.stem: A patient on 100% O2 has PaO2 falling from 450 to 150 mmHg, but SpO2 stays 100%. What limitation does this show?
options: SpO2 gives no early warning of falling PaO2
The probe is malpositioned on the finger
Pulse oximetry overestimates PaO2 at all levels
questions.explanation: Above roughly 90 mmHg, the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve is nearly flat. PaO₂ can fall markedly while SpO₂ remains close to 100%, so saturation does not quantify oxygen reserve.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 253 (textbook passage reviewed)

questions.stem: Pulse oximetry became standard of care in what year?
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry became a routine intraoperative standard in 1986 after improved sensors and digital processing made continuous monitoring practical.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11, printed p. 255 (textbook passage reviewed)

questions.stem: Where is hypoxemia more common?
options: Neither; hypoxemia is rare after surgery
questions.explanation: Patients in the postanesthesia care unit remain at risk for hypoxemia from residual anesthetic effects, airway obstruction, and atelectasis. The exact comparison with the operating room depends on the population and monitoring conditions.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8: Respiratory Gas Monitoring; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 18: Clinical Monitoring II: Respiratory and Metabolic Systems [Exact supporting passage/page not independently verified]

questions.stem: Which patient factors are associated with postoperative desaturation? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Obesity, older age, and extensive surgery can increase the risk of postoperative desaturation through reduced respiratory reserve, residual anesthetic effects, and postoperative ventilation changes.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8: Respiratory Gas Monitoring; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 18: Clinical Monitoring II: Respiratory and Metabolic Systems [Exact supporting passage/page not independently verified]

questions.stem: Which situation is a classic setup for postoperative desaturation?
options: Supine position with O2 by mask
Arrival in PACU on a nonrebreather
Transport to PACU without supplemental O2
questions.explanation: Transport without supplemental oxygen may unmask limited respiratory reserve after anesthesia. Assess oxygenation and ventilation during transfer and provide oxygen when clinically indicated.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 11: Pulse Oximetry; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 18: Clinical Monitoring II: Respiratory and Metabolic Systems [Exact supporting passage/page not independently verified]

questions.stem: Peak pressure rises suddenly with a shark-fin capnogram. Which cause fits both?
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm increases expiratory airway resistance, often raising peak airway pressure and producing a slow, slanted capnogram upstroke. A kinked tube can mimic this pattern and should also be excluded.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed pp 241–242 (textbook passage reviewed)

questions.stem: Airway pressure and EtCO2 both fall to near zero suddenly. Most likely cause?
questions.explanation: A circuit disconnection can abruptly eliminate measured airway pressure and the exhaled CO₂ waveform. Immediately assess the patient, breathing circuit, and airway rather than assuming monitor failure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 10, printed p. 241 (textbook passage reviewed)

questions.stem: Infrared analyzers are categorized as which two types?
questions.explanation: Infrared gas analyzers are classified as dispersive or nondispersive. Dispersive systems separate wavelengths into a spectrum; nondispersive systems select specific wavelength bands with filters.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 200 (textbook passage reviewed)

questions.stem: The process of eliminating CO2 is called:
questions.explanation: Ventilation exchanges alveolar gas and eliminates metabolically produced CO₂. Oxygenation refers to transfer of oxygen into blood; the two processes are related but distinct.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 149–160 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Gas solubility in a liquid is directly proportional to its partial pressure above the liquid. This is:
questions.explanation: Henry's law relates dissolved gas concentration to the partial pressure of that gas above a liquid at constant temperature. Dalton's law instead describes partial pressures within a gas mixture.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 149–160 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: How does systemic vascular tone respond to low O2 or high CO2?
questions.explanation: Hypoxia and hypercapnia generally promote vasodilation in the systemic circulation. Pulmonary arterioles respond differently to local alveolar hypoxia, typically constricting.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 149–160 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Filling the lungs with O2 so tissues are supplied without ventilation is called:
questions.explanation: Apneic oxygenation supplies oxygen to alveoli despite absent tidal breathing, provided the airway remains patent. It does not adequately remove CO₂, which continues to accumulate.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 149–160 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: During spontaneous inspiration, diaphragm contraction makes intrathoracic pressure:
questions.explanation: Diaphragm contraction increases thoracic volume and lowers intrathoracic pressure below atmospheric pressure, drawing gas into the lungs.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 149–160 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Change in lung volume per change in pressure is called:
questions.explanation: Compliance measures the change in lung or respiratory-system volume per unit change in distending pressure: C = ΔV/ΔP. Lower compliance means a stiffer system.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 149–160 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Pulmonary fibrosis has what effect on compliance?
options: Increases it only at high volumes
questions.explanation: Fibrosis reduces lung compliance because stiffened lung tissue requires a greater pressure change to produce the same volume change.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 149–160 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Bronchoconstriction or ETT obstruction has what effect on resistance?
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm or a narrowed endotracheal tube increases resistance to airflow. More driving pressure is needed to maintain the same flow.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 149–160 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Volume equals:
questions.explanation: For constant flow, delivered volume equals flow multiplied by elapsed time. With a changing flow waveform, volume is the area under the flow–time curve.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 149–160 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Flow multiplied by resistance gives:
questions.explanation: For a given flow under a simplified resistive model, the resistive pressure drop is flow multiplied by resistance. This excludes the elastic and baseline pressure components.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 149–160 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Airway pressure equals:
questions.explanation: The simplified equation of motion adds resistive pressure (flow × resistance), elastic pressure (volume/compliance), and baseline PEEP. Patient effort and dynamic effects can modify actual airway pressure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 149–160 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Alveolar pressure equals:
questions.explanation: At zero airway flow during an inspiratory hold, the resistive pressure drop falls to zero. Plateau pressure approximates the elastic pressure (volume/compliance) plus PEEP.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 149–160 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: A patient develops bronchospasm during volume control. Which term of the airway pressure equation rises?
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm increases airway resistance, raising the resistive contribution to peak inspiratory pressure during volume control. Plateau pressure may remain relatively unchanged.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 149–160 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Pneumoperitoneum is established during volume control. Which term of the airway pressure equation rises most?
questions.explanation: Pneumoperitoneum can decrease respiratory-system compliance, so delivering the same tidal volume requires more elastic distending pressure and can increase plateau pressure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 149–160 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Which are the four main components of a mechanical ventilator? Select 3.
questions.explanation: A ventilator needs a power source and controls, and must incorporate monitoring and safety protections. This select-three item lists only three of those four categories as correct options.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 149–160 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: A piston ventilator's drive force comes from:
questions.explanation: A piston ventilator uses an electrically driven motor to displace a piston and deliver the programmed breath. It does not require pneumatic driving gas in the same way as a conventional bellows.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: A bellows ventilator's drive force comes from:
options: An electric motor moving a piston
Compressed driving gas squeezing the bellows
questions.explanation: A conventional double-circuit bellows ventilator uses compressed driving gas outside the bellows to compress it and deliver patient gas during inspiration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Ascending bellows rise during which phase?
questions.explanation: In an ascending-bellows design, the bellows rises as the patient exhales into the circuit and refills the bellows during expiration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: What happens to ascending bellows with a circuit disconnection?
options: They rise normally from room air entrainment
They fail to rise fully or collapse
They lock in the inspiratory position
questions.explanation: With a significant disconnection, an ascending bellows generally fails to refill completely and may collapse, providing a visual warning in addition to electronic alarms.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: What happens to descending bellows with a circuit disconnection?
options: They rise to the top of the housing
They stop moving and lock in place
They still fill with room air and look normal
They collapse immediately and stay down
questions.explanation: A descending bellows may continue descending or appear filled despite a circuit disconnection because gravity and entrained gas can mask lost exhaled volume. Electronic alarms remain essential.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Why are ascending bellows considered safer for detecting disconnection?
options: They have a higher relief valve opening pressure
They entrain room air during a disconnect
They use an electric motor as the drive
Ascending bellows need exhaled gas to rise
questions.explanation: Ascending bellows rely on returned exhaled gas to refill. Incomplete rise can therefore indicate circuit disconnection, although electronic pressure and volume alarms are still necessary.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: The ascending bellows spill (relief) valve opens at about what pressure?
questions.explanation: A bellows spill valve permits excess circuit gas to enter scavenging during expiration. Its opening pressure varies with ventilator and valve design; the quoted 2–4 cmH₂O is model-specific.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: What side effect does the ascending bellows spill valve produce?
options: A small amount of baseline PEEP
questions.explanation: The pressure needed to open an ascending-bellows spill valve may create a small expiratory backpressure. The amount depends on the particular system and should not be assumed universal.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Which safety features help detect disconnection with descending bellows on newer machines? Select 3.
options: Sensors detecting failure to return to full hang
A spill valve opening at 75 cmH2O
questions.explanation: Descending bellows do not reliably reveal disconnection by appearance alone. Pressure, expired-volume, capnography, and appropriate system sensors help detect inadequate ventilation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Which are consequences of a hole in the bellows? Select 3.
options: Altered FiO2 depending on drive gas
Lower airway pressure at the patient
questions.explanation: A leak separating driving gas from the patient circuit can introduce driving gas into inspired gas, changing oxygen and volatile-agent concentrations and potentially affecting delivered pressure or volume.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: A bellows leak develops on a machine using 100% O2 as drive gas. How does FiO2 change?
options: It falls only if N2O is in use
questions.explanation: If pure oxygen is used as driving gas and leaks into the patient circuit, the inspired oxygen fraction may rise while inhaled anesthetic is diluted.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: A bellows leak develops on a machine using an air/O2 drive gas while delivering 100% O2. How does FiO2 change?
questions.explanation: If the driving gas contains air, a leak into a circuit delivering pure oxygen can lower inspired oxygen concentration and dilute volatile anesthetic.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Expired agent drops unexpectedly with ascending bellows and normal vaporizer function. Which equipment problem fits?
options: Bellows leak releasing agent on expiration
questions.explanation: A bellows leak can cause unexpectedly low inspired or expired anesthetic concentration through dilution or loss of anesthetic-containing gas. The exact pattern depends on ventilator design.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Which ventilator does NOT need driving gas?
options: Pneumatic bellows with an air drive
questions.explanation: An electrically driven piston supplies mechanical force directly to the circuit without consuming a separate compressed pneumatic driving-gas supply.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: During an O2 pipeline failure with only a cylinder available, which ventilator type conserves O2 best?
options: Any bellows ventilator with high FGF
Piston, since it needs no driving gas
questions.explanation: An electric piston can conserve available cylinder oxygen during loss of pipeline supply because it does not require oxygen for pneumatic drive, assuming its electrical power remains available.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: A piston ventilator's positive pressure relief valve opens at:
questions.explanation: Positive-pressure relief valves limit excess circuit pressure, but a 75 cmH₂O opening threshold applies to specific piston machines rather than all piston ventilators.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: A piston ventilator's negative pressure relief valve opens at:
questions.explanation: A negative-pressure relief valve protects against excessive subatmospheric circuit pressure. The −8 cmH₂O threshold depends on the model.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: A piston's negative pressure relief valve opens repeatedly during a case with low FGF. What is the main risk?
options: Room air entrainment dilutes agent, risking awareness
Rising agent concentration in the circuit
questions.explanation: If negative circuit pressure opens a relief valve, room air may enter, lowering inspired oxygen and volatile-agent concentrations. This can compromise anesthetic delivery.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Negative end-expiratory pressure (NEEP) is a recognized risk of which ventilator?
questions.explanation: Some piston systems can create subatmospheric pressure during portions of the respiratory cycle. Negative-pressure protection and correct circuit setup are important.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 160–174 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Fresh gas decoupling is a feature of which ventilator type?
questions.explanation: Fresh-gas decoupling is used in certain piston systems to prevent continuous fresh-gas flow from adding unintended volume during inspiration. It is not exclusive to every piston design.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 172–177 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: During inspiration with fresh gas decoupling, where does fresh gas go?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, a fresh-gas decoupling valve diverts incoming fresh gas away from the patient breath and into a reservoir bag.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 172–177 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: During expiration with fresh gas decoupling, where does fresh gas go?
options: Out to the scavenger through the APL
Into the reservoir bag, bypassing the piston
Into the piston to fill it for the next breath
questions.explanation: During expiration, the decoupling valve permits reservoir and fresh gas to replenish the piston chamber for the next programmed breath.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 172–177 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: With fresh gas decoupling, raising FGF from 2 to 8 L/min changes delivered tidal volume how?
options: It increases with the extra flow
It decreases as gas is vented
questions.explanation: Fresh-gas decoupling separates fresh-gas inflow from the delivered inspiratory volume, so changing fresh-gas flow should not directly increase the programmed tidal volume when the system functions correctly.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 172–177 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Without fresh gas decoupling, raising FGF during volume control has what effect on delivered tidal volume?
options: It has no effect on delivered volume
It decreases only at high respiratory rates
It increases, because fresh gas adds to each breath
It decreases, because the extra fresh gas is vented
questions.explanation: Without fresh-gas decoupling or compensation, incoming fresh gas during inspiration can add to the ventilator's delivered breath and increase tidal volume.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 172–177 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Which are benefits of fresh gas decoupling? Select 2.
options: Higher delivered Vt at high FGF
questions.explanation: Decoupling improves tidal-volume consistency despite changes in fresh-gas flow and supports efficient low-flow anesthesia when the workstation is correctly configured.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 172–177 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: In a decoupled piston circuit, the reservoir bag inflates and deflates with each breath during mechanical ventilation. What does this reflect?
options: The APL valve is stuck in the closed position
The decoupling valve has failed in the open position
Normal function of a decoupled piston system
A disconnection at the Y-piece is present
questions.explanation: In a decoupled piston system the reservoir bag collects fresh gas during inspiration and empties toward the piston during expiration. Its cyclic movement is expected.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 172–177 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of a piston ventilator?
options: It adapts easily to non-rebreathing circuits
It is loud, so cycling is easy to hear
It adds no PEEP to the system
questions.explanation: Unlike ascending bellows, a piston does not inherently generate expiratory backpressure from a bellows spill valve. Actual PEEP depends on the workstation settings and design.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 172–177 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Which are disadvantages of piston ventilators? Select 3.
options: Adds a baseline PEEP to the system
Requires O2 as its driving gas
Quiet, so cycling may not be heard
Not easily adapted to non-rebreathing circuits
questions.explanation: Piston systems may generate negative pressure, operate quietly, and have circuit-compatibility limitations. These disadvantages depend on the specific workstation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 172–177 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Why do piston ventilators deliver more precise tidal volumes?
options: Compliance/leak compensation and fresh gas decoupling
Absence of a reservoir bag anywhere in the circuit
A spill valve that adds a little PEEP
Higher driving gas pressure in the housing
questions.explanation: Piston position control supports accurate displacement, while fresh-gas decoupling and compliance/leak compensation reduce differences between set and delivered tidal volume.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 172–177 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: A turbine ventilator raises circuit pressure during inspiration by doing what?
options: Opening a solenoid to the pipeline
Moving a piston with a motor
questions.explanation: A turbine creates inspiratory pressure and flow by changing its rotational speed. Higher turbine speed generally produces greater driving pressure.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 172–177 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Which are listed benefits of turbine ventilators? Select 2.
options: Built-in negative pressure protection at −8 cmH2O
Added PEEP from a spill valve
Use of O2 as drive gas
questions.explanation: Turbine systems can support precise gas delivery and mixing, but claims of reduced dead space or universally improved mixing depend on the particular workstation design.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 172–177 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Solenoid valves control gas flow by:
options: A bimetallic strip that bends with heat
A float rising in a tapered tube
Pneumatic pressure from the pipeline only
An electric current creating a magnetic field
questions.explanation: A solenoid valve uses an electromagnetic field generated by electric current to actuate a valve and control gas flow or timing.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 172–177 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: Which cycling mechanism do most anesthesia ventilators use in controlled modes?
questions.explanation: In time-cycled mandatory ventilation, inspiration ends after a preset inspiratory time. Whether most current anesthesia modes are time-cycled depends on how the triggering, limiting and cycling definitions are applied.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 172–177 (chapter section reviewed; question-specific confirmation pending where flagged)

questions.stem: In time-cycled ventilation, what ends inspiration?
options: Flow falling to a preset value
questions.explanation: Time-cycled inspiration ends when the preset inspiratory time has elapsed. Respiratory rate and the I:E ratio determine the time available for each phase.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 162

questions.stem: Which is a drawback of time-cycled controlled ventilation?
options: Ventilation stops with low respiratory drive
questions.explanation: Unsynchronized controlled breaths can conflict with spontaneous effort and cause dyssynchrony. The question is ambiguous because time-cycled pressure control can also produce compliance-dependent tidal volumes, making another option plausible.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed pp. 277–278

questions.stem: In flow-cycled ventilation, inspiration ends when:
options: Flow drops to a preset value
questions.explanation: Flow cycling ends inspiration when inspiratory flow falls to the selected threshold. The pressure-support example in Figure 6.22 uses a fraction of peak flow rather than a fixed inspiratory duration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 162; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 168

questions.stem: In the pressure-support example shown in Figure 6.22, inspiration ends when flow falls to approximately what fraction of peak inspiratory flow?
questions.explanation: The pressure-support flow trace in Figure 6.22 labels the cycling threshold as 25% of peak inspiratory flow. This is a figure-specific example, not a universal setting for every ventilator.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 6, printed p. 168 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: How does poor compliance affect tidal volume in flow-cycled modes?
questions.explanation: At fixed pressure support, reduced respiratory-system compliance can reduce tidal volume. Flow cycling alone does not specify pressure, patient effort, or other settings, so the broad wording needs qualification.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 152, 166, 168

questions.stem: During constant-flow volume-controlled ventilation, which variable changes when lung compliance or airway resistance changes while set flow and tidal volume remain fixed?
questions.explanation: In constant-flow volume control, the ventilator maintains the selected flow pattern and tidal volume. Airway pressure rises when resistance increases or compliance decreases.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Ch. 6, printed p. 153 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Older pressure-cycled ventilators have what drawback with poor compliance?
options: Increased pneumothorax risk from fixed volume
questions.explanation: A pressure-cycled ventilator ends inspiration when the selected pressure is reached. With reduced compliance, that pressure can be reached after a smaller volume has entered the lungs, reducing tidal volume.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 152, 162

questions.stem: Per the instructor, what FiO2 is typical during maintenance?
questions.explanation: Maintenance FiO₂ is adjusted to the patient’s oxygenation and procedural risks. The inspected passage does not establish 30–50% as a universal maintenance range, so the keyed number remains unverified.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Why use a low FiO2 during maintenance?
options: Reduce airway fire risk and O2 toxicity
questions.explanation: Unnecessary high oxygen concentrations increase exposure in patients susceptible to oxygen toxicity and can increase airway fire risk near an ignition source. Oxygen must still be sufficient for adequate oxygenation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 211

questions.stem: When are high FiO2 values appropriate? Select 2.
options: Routine maintenance of a healthy patient
questions.explanation: High inspired oxygen is used during preoxygenation to replace lung nitrogen and increase the oxygen reserve before airway management. The inspected passage supports that choice but does not independently verify routine emergence as the second answer.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 8, printed p. 211

questions.stem: What initial adult respiratory-rate range does Nurse Anesthesia list for volume-controlled ventilation, with subsequent titration to end-tidal CO₂?
questions.explanation: Nurse Anesthesia lists an initial adult volume-control rate of 6–12 breaths per minute. The rate should then be adjusted to the measured end-tidal CO₂ and the patient's ventilation needs.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Ch. 16, printed p. 277 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Per the instructor, EtCO2 typically runs how much below PaCO2?
questions.explanation: End-tidal CO₂ is approximately 2–5 mmHg below arterial CO₂ in patients without cardiopulmonary abnormalities. Increased dead space or hemodynamic changes can widen this difference, so the approximation is conditional.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 18, printed p. 316

questions.stem: Near emergence, why might you lower the ventilator rate?
options: Allow CO2 to rise and stimulate respiratory drive
Lower CO2 to deepen the anesthetic before waking
questions.explanation: Reducing alveolar ventilation can increase PaCO₂ because less metabolic CO₂ is eliminated. The proposed use of a lower mandatory rate to restore respiratory drive during emergence still requires a specific supporting passage.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 151

questions.stem: When low tidal volume ventilation is used, what often must change to manage CO2?
questions.explanation: Reducing tidal volume reduces minute ventilation unless respiratory rate increases. A higher rate may therefore be needed to preserve alveolar ventilation and CO₂ elimination, with allowance for dead-space ventilation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 151–153

questions.stem: Laparoscopic CO2 insufflation tends to do what to EtCO2 at constant ventilation?
questions.explanation: Absorbed insufflation CO₂ increases the amount of CO₂ the lungs must eliminate. At fixed minute ventilation, pneumoperitoneum can therefore raise both arterial and end-tidal CO₂.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 34, printed p. 809

questions.stem: Lengthening inspiratory time (increasing the I:E ratio) mainly improves what?
options: CO2 clearance from the alveoli each breath
questions.explanation: Lengthening inspiration can increase mean airway pressure and recruit collapsed alveoli, improving oxygenation in selected patients. Shorter expiration also increases the risk of incomplete emptying and auto-PEEP.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 159–160

questions.stem: Which are effects of lengthening inspiratory time? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Lengthening inspiration shortens expiration and can cause incomplete emptying, auto-PEEP, and impaired venous return. Reduced CO₂ elimination is conditional, so the complete three-answer set remains unverified.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 160

questions.stem: Lengthening expiratory time (decreasing the I:E ratio) mainly improves what?
options: CO2 clearance and less air trapping
questions.explanation: Longer expiration gives obstructed lungs more time to empty and can reduce air trapping. Improved CO₂ clearance is not automatic because it also depends on effective alveolar ventilation.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 644

questions.stem: A COPD patient shows rising peak pressures and expiratory flow that doesn't reach zero. Best I:E change?
questions.explanation: Expiratory flow that fails to reach zero suggests incomplete emptying and intrinsic PEEP. Increasing the time for expiration, for example by changing from 1:2 to 1:3, addresses this mechanism.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 644

questions.stem: The default I:E ratio for mechanical ventilation is:
questions.explanation: An I:E ratio of 1:2 is a typical initial adult volume-control setting in the text. It is a starting point that must be adjusted for respiratory mechanics and incomplete expiration.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Which I:E range suits obstructive lung disease?
questions.explanation: Obstructive disease commonly needs a longer expiratory time to limit gas trapping. The principle supports a lower I:E ratio, but the exact 1:3–1:4 range is not verified by the inspected passage.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 644

questions.stem: Which inspiratory-to-expiratory (I:E) ratio range is listed in the ARDS Network ventilation protocol in Nurse Anesthesia Table 29.25?
questions.explanation: Table 29.25 lists an I:E range of 1:1 to 1:3 for the ARDS Network ventilation protocol. This is a protocol range, not a universal I:E requirement for all patients with ARDS.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Ch. 29, printed p. 669 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Increasing inspiratory flow rate while keeping RR and Vt constant has what effect?
options: Shortens inspiratory time and lengthens expiratory time
Lengthens both inspiratory and expiratory time
Leaves inspiratory and expiratory time unchanged
Lengthens inspiratory time and shortens expiration
questions.explanation: At fixed tidal volume, increasing constant inspiratory flow delivers the volume in less time. If respiratory rate and pause time are unchanged, the shorter inspiration leaves more time for expiration.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 153–154

questions.stem: An inspiratory pause (plateau) is thought to improve what?
questions.explanation: An inspiratory pause holds the delivered volume after flow stops, allowing gas redistribution and keeping alveoli expanded longer. This may reduce shunt and improve oxygenation, while also permitting assessment of static compliance.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 164

questions.stem: The recommended tidal volume is about:
questions.explanation: A protective ventilation strategy can use tidal volumes of 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight. This limits excessive lung stretch; the target is adjusted for the patient and ventilation strategy rather than actual body mass.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 159; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 34, printed pp. 809–810

questions.stem: Tidal volume should be calculated from which weight?
options: Adjusted body weight for all patients
questions.explanation: Tidal volume is selected using ideal or predicted body weight in the inspected ventilation guidance. This avoids increasing the tidal-volume target merely because actual body weight is higher.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Set Vt 500 mL, circuit compliance 4 mL/cmH2O, PIP 25 cmH2O. Using the lecture formula, about what Vt is delivered?
questions.explanation: Assuming zero baseline pressure and no compensation or fresh-gas contribution, circuit volume loss is 4 × 25 = 100 mL. Subtracting this from 500 mL gives approximately 400 mL delivered to the patient.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 103; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 152, 165

questions.stem: Circuit compliance stays the same but PIP doubles. How does the volume lost to the circuit change?
questions.explanation: At constant compliance, circuit expansion volume is proportional to the pressure rise across the breath. Doubling PIP doubles this loss only when the relevant pressure rise also doubles; a nonzero PEEP baseline can change the calculation.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 4, printed p. 103; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152

questions.stem: Which are suggested benefits of low tidal volume ventilation? Select 3.
options: Higher EtCO2 at the same rate is desirable
Lower risk of atelectasis without PEEP
questions.explanation: Lower tidal volumes reduce mortality in ARDS, and protective ventilation bundles can improve postoperative outcomes. The passages do not isolate all three listed benefits as effects of low tidal volume alone, so the complete key remains unresolved.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 159; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 34, printed pp. 809–810

questions.stem: Which trigger method do anesthesia ventilators typically use?
questions.explanation: A flow trigger detects patient effort through a change in circuit flow. Both pressure and flow triggering are described in the text, but the inspected passages do not establish 2 L/min as a universal anesthesia-ventilator setting.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 162, 168

questions.stem: Which trigger type is most sensitive?
questions.explanation: Pressure and flow triggers both detect patient effort, and their thresholds affect responsiveness. The inspected passage does not establish flow triggering as universally the most sensitive method.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 168

questions.stem: Trigger sensitivity is set too high (very hard to trigger). What happens?
options: The patient's work of breathing increases
The patient’s work of breathing decreases
PEEP is lost from the circuit
questions.explanation: A trigger that is difficult to activate requires the patient to generate more inspiratory effort before assistance begins. The parenthetical definition in the stem matters because numerical sensitivity labels vary between ventilators.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 278

questions.stem: Trigger sensitivity is set too low (very easy to trigger). What happens?
options: The patient must work harder to start each breath
The ventilator may trigger without a true patient effort
Triggered breaths fail to be delivered
questions.explanation: If a trigger responds too easily, motion in the surgical field can initiate a breath without a true patient inspiration. Adjusting the trigger threshold or window can reduce this false triggering.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 278

questions.stem: A pressure trigger example in the lecture is about:
questions.explanation: Pressure triggering begins assistance after the patient creates the required negative airway-pressure deflection. The selected threshold depends on the ventilator and patient; the inspected passages do not verify −3 cmH₂O as the specified example.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 168; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 278

questions.stem: The default PEEP is:
questions.explanation: PEEP helps prevent alveolar collapse and is selected for the patient’s lung mechanics and oxygenation. The text includes ranges beginning at 5 cmH₂O, but it does not establish 5 as the universal ventilator default.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: When titrating PEEP, the lecture suggests increasing by about:
questions.explanation: PEEP can recruit alveoli, but excessive PEEP may overdistend them and impair venous return. The inspected text does not verify the stated increment, interval, or upper limit, so that numerical protocol needs review.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 159, 164

questions.stem: Which are risks of high PEEP? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Excessive PEEP can reduce venous return and cardiac output, and overdistension can contribute to barotrauma. The third keyed claim about increased intracranial pressure requires separate source verification.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 159, 164

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of PEEP?
options: Shorten expiratory time to clear CO2
Prevent alveolar collapse and improve oxygenation
Increase CO2 elimination from the alveoli
questions.explanation: PEEP helps keep recruitable alveoli open at end expiration, improving oxygenation. Excessive PEEP may overdistend already open alveoli without recruiting additional lung units.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 159, 164

questions.stem: According to Nurse Anesthesia Table 16.7, what peak inspiratory pressure (PIP) limit is listed as a lung-protection target?
questions.explanation: Table 16.7 lists a peak inspiratory pressure target below 35 cm H₂O. It separately lists plateau pressure below 28 cm H₂O and driving pressure below 16 cm H₂O; these measurements should not be conflated.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Ch. 16, printed p. 277 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Per the instructor, a typical PIP for a healthy patient is about:
questions.explanation: Peak inspiratory pressure depends on tidal volume, inspiratory flow, resistance, compliance, and baseline pressure. The inspected passages do not establish 13–20 cmH₂O as a universal healthy-patient range.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed pp. 152, 166

questions.stem: Which cause increased PIP through increased airway resistance? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm, mucus plugging, and biting the endotracheal tube narrow the gas pathway and increase resistance. During volume control, more resistive pressure is needed to deliver the same flow, raising PIP.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 166; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Which cause increased PIP through decreased lung compliance? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Pneumoperitoneum, steep Trendelenburg, and atelectatic lung can reduce respiratory-system compliance. At a fixed delivered volume, a stiffer system requires greater inflation pressure.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed pp. 277, 809–810

questions.stem: Which cause PIP to decrease? Select 3.
questions.explanation: Bronchodilation reduces resistance, and release of pneumoperitoneum can improve compliance, lowering pressure during comparable volume-controlled breaths. A leak or disconnect can also reduce pressure, but its displayed effect depends on ventilator compensation, leaving the broad three-answer key conditional.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 152; Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: PIP suddenly drops from 22 to 8 cmH2O during volume control, and exhaled Vt falls. FIRST action?
options: Check for a disconnection or leak
questions.explanation: A sudden decrease in PIP together with a fall in returned tidal volume is consistent with a leak or disconnection. Check the patient, airway, and breathing circuit immediately rather than assuming improved lung mechanics.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed p. 277

questions.stem: Switching from volume control to pressure control usually has what effect on displayed PIP?
questions.explanation: Pressure control may provide the desired volume at lower peak pressure in selected patients. A switch alone does not guarantee a decrease: the comparison depends on the pressure target, delivered volume, flow pattern, and respiratory mechanics.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 16, printed pp. 277–278

questions.stem: During laparoscopy, which physiologic change can raise peak inspiratory pressure during volume-controlled ventilation after pneumoperitoneum?
questions.explanation: Pneumoperitoneum can reduce respiratory-system compliance, so higher pressure is needed to deliver the same tidal volume in volume control. The prior fixed 38-cm H₂O intervention threshold and duplicate disconnection choices were unsupported.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Ch. 16, printed p. 277 (complete revised answer independently verified against inspected passage)

questions.stem: Plateau pressure is measured when?
questions.explanation: Plateau pressure is assessed during an end-inspiratory pause after airflow has ceased. This removes the pressure contribution from ongoing flow through airway resistance.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 620; Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6, printed p. 164

questions.stem: Plateau pressure best reflects what?
questions.explanation: During a no-flow inspiratory hold, plateau pressure reflects elastic pressure in the respiratory system together with baseline PEEP. It therefore relates more closely to lung and chest-wall compliance than to flow-dependent airway resistance.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed pp. 620–621

questions.stem: Static compliance is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Static compliance is tidal volume divided by plateau pressure minus PEEP: Cstat = VT/(Pplat − PEEP). It is assessed under no-flow conditions so the pressure reflects elastic rather than resistive loading.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 620

questions.stem: Dynamic compliance is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Dynamic compliance is VT/(PIP − PEEP). Because PIP is measured during flow, this value incorporates airway resistance as well as respiratory-system elastic properties.
questions.citation: Elisha, Heiner, & Nagelhout (2023), Nurse Anesthesia, 7th ed., Chapter 29, printed p. 621

questions.stem: Vt 500 mL, Pplat 25 cmH2O, PEEP 5 cmH2O. Static compliance?
questions.explanation: Static respiratory-system compliance is tidal volume divided by plateau pressure minus total PEEP. Here, 500/(25−5) = 25 mL/cmH₂O.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6: Anesthesia Ventilators [chapter reference; exact answer-specific page not verified]

questions.stem: Vt 600 mL, PIP 35, Pplat 20, PEEP 5 cmH2O. Dynamic compliance?
questions.explanation: Dynamic compliance uses peak inspiratory pressure while flow is present: 600/(35−5) = 20 mL/cmH₂O. Plateau pressure would instead estimate static compliance.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6: Anesthesia Ventilators [chapter reference; exact answer-specific page not verified]

questions.stem: Driving pressure equals:
questions.explanation: Driving pressure is plateau pressure minus total PEEP during passive ventilation. It reflects the pressure associated with delivering the tidal breath.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6: Anesthesia Ventilators [chapter reference; exact answer-specific page not verified]

questions.stem: Which strategy keeps plateau pressure low to reduce ventilator-induced lung injury?
options: Higher tidal volume with zero PEEP
Lower tidal volume with reasonable PEEP
questions.explanation: Lower tidal volumes reduce alveolar overdistension. PEEP should be individualized to maintain recruitment without excessive pressure or hemodynamic compromise.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6: Anesthesia Ventilators [chapter reference; exact answer-specific page not verified]

questions.stem: On this pressure-time waveform, which numbered point is the plateau pressure?
questions.explanation: Plateau pressure is measured during an inspiratory pause when airflow has stopped. The textbook establishes the principle; confirm that the image labels this as point 2.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6: Anesthesia Ventilators [chapter reference; exact answer-specific page not verified]

questions.stem: On this waveform, the difference between points 1 and 2 reflects what?
options: The PEEP level set on the vent
A leak in the circuit or cuff
questions.explanation: Peak-to-plateau pressure difference estimates resistive pressure under constant flow, whereas plateau minus PEEP estimates driving pressure. Verify the figure's numbered points.
questions.citation: Ehrenwerth, Eisenkraft, & Berry (2021), Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, 3rd ed., Chapter 6: Anesthesia Ventilators [chapter reference; exact answer-specific page not verified]

questions.stem: On this waveform, which pair of points gives driving pressure?
